analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards and shortens deadlines for people injured by defective products, and shields implant-material suppliers from most lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Senate came close in July 1998 but fell 9 votes short of cutting off debate on an amendment (51–47, with 60 needed), and the bill died without a final vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the product liability laws of all 50 states with one federal set of rules, mostly written around the concerns of companies being sued. It would have capped punitive damages at the greater of twice the compensatory award or $250,000, required a high 'clear and convincing' standard of proof for punitive damages, given injured people only two years to sue after discovering an injury, barred most suits about products more than 18 years old, ended joint liability so each company pays only its own percentage of pain-and-suffering awards, and shielded suppliers of raw materials used in medical implants from almost all liability. Supporters said the patchwork of state laws raised prices for everyone; opponents said its main effect was to make it harder and cheaper for companies to be held accountable for injuring people.
analysis.who_benefits: Product manufacturers and sellers benefit most: caps on punitive damages, tighter deadlines, an 18-year cutoff on older-product claims, and an end to joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards all lower their worst-case litigation costs. Liability insurers benefit because payouts shrink and become more predictable. Suppliers of raw materials and parts used in medical implants benefit from near-total immunity unless they violated contract specifications. Retailers and rental companies gain from rules limiting seller liability to cases of negligence, express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing.

how_it_helps.text: Punitive damages would require proof by clear and convincing evidence of conduct showing 'conscious, flagrant indifference' to safety, and would be capped at the greater of twice compensatory damages or $250,000 [S2] [S3].

Lawsuits generally must be filed within two years of discovering the harm, and suits about products delivered more than 18 years earlier are barred (with exceptions for passenger transport vehicles and longer written warranties) [S2] [S3].
Each defendant would pay only its own proportional share of noneconomic damages such as pain and suffering, instead of being jointly liable for the whole award when others cannot pay [S2] [S3].

Sellers, renters, and lessors who did not make the product would be liable only for negligence, breach of an express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing, and a failure to inspect would not count as negligence when no reasonable opportunity to inspect existed [S2] [S3].
Intoxication would be a complete defense if the injured person was under the influence and more than 50 percent responsible for the event [S2] [S3].

Suppliers of raw materials and parts for medical implants would be immune from suit in nearly all cases, limited to liability when they are the manufacturer, resold the implant, or furnished materials that failed contract specifications, plus fee-shifting against claimants whose suits against suppliers are found frivolous [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products bear the cost: lower and harder-to-win punitive awards, shorter filing windows that can expire before a latent injury is understood, loss of joint liability when a judgment-proof defendant leaves a share of the harm unpaid, and almost no recourse against implant-material suppliers.

drawbacks.text: The caps and deadlines would reduce recovery for the most severely injured people precisely in the cases involving the worst corporate conduct, since the highest punitive awards are the ones capped [S2] [S3].

The bill overrides state law nationwide, including in states whose legislatures and courts had deliberately chosen stronger protections for injured consumers, applying to cases in any state or federal court [S2] [S3].

Ending joint liability for noneconomic loss means that when one responsible company cannot pay a judgment, the injured person absorbs the uncovered share of their own pain-and-suffering damages [S2] [S3].
The 18-year cutoff would bar claims about long-lasting products that cause harm decades after delivery, although suits involving toxic harm are exempt from that particular bar [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument on the supporters' side: inconsistent state rules create uncertainty for companies selling nationwide, and some liability costs do get passed to consumers in prices, while the biomaterials provisions respond to a documented problem of raw-material suppliers exiting the medical-implant market over litigation exposure. But the bill's center of gravity is a one-way reduction in what companies pay when their products injure people: caps, deadlines, higher proof standards, and immunity provisions all cut in one direction, and nothing in it strengthens remedies for injured consumers. Its main effect would have been shifting the cost of defective products from companies to the people they hurt.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate took the bill up in July 1998, but a vote to end debate on an amendment failed 51–47 with 60 votes needed, every Democrat opposed, so the bill went back to the calendar and never came up for a final vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in April 1997 by Sen. Slade Gorton with 10 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S4] [S5].
The Commerce Committee reported it favorably without amendment in June 1997, with minority views filed by committee members who disagreed, and it was placed on the Senate calendar [S5].
In July 1998 the Senate invoked cloture on a motion to proceed — a vote to allow the bill to be considered at all — by 71–24, with 50 Republicans and 21 Democrats in favor [S6] [S5].

Two days later, cloture on Amendment SP 3064 failed 51–47: all 51 voting Republicans but two voted yes, and all 45 Democrats voted no; because 60 votes were needed, debate could not be cut off and the bill was returned to the calendar [S7] [S5].
The bill remained on the calendar with no final Senate vote and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products are better off, because they kept whatever rights their state laws give them to sue for full damages. Product manufacturers, sellers, and liability insurers are also better off in the sense that they avoided a federal cap they had sought, but they gained nothing new — the outcome preserved the legal status quo they wanted changed.

sides.party_line_note: The decisive July 9, 1998 vote split almost entirely by party — 51 of 53 voting Republicans for cutting off debate, 0 of 45 Democrats for it — though two days earlier the vote to proceed had been bipartisan, with 21 of 42 voting Democrats joining 50 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would cap punitive awards, shorten filing deadlines, end joint liability for pain and suffering, and largely insulate non-manufacturer sellers — each lowering what companies pay when their products hurt people. The bill's own findings argue this lowers consumer prices, but the direct effect is to reduce compensation to injured buyers.

Caps, deadlines, and higher proof standards shrink and stabilize claim payouts, which benefits insurers writing product liability coverage. Insured companies' savings and injured people's losses are two sides of the same transfer.

industries.industry: Medical implant raw-material and component suppliers
industries.note: Title II would make suppliers of biomaterials essentially immune from implant-injury suits except when they breach contract specifications, converting them from potential defendants into protected suppliers. The bill itself cites suppliers exiting the market over litigation risk; silicone breast implant claimants are carved out of this shield [S2] [S3].

Fewer viable claims, shorter windows, capped damages, and fee-shifting against frivolous suits against implant suppliers would directly reduce contingency-fee litigation business. The same mechanisms are what injured consumers lose.
